draftPackage.topic: The wooden receipts behind Parliament’s 1834 fire
draftPackage.centralQuestion: How did disposing of obsolete wooden receipts help destroy the old Palace of Westminster?
draftPackage.thesis: A record system became obsolete; furnace disposal of its wooden leftovers caused a chimney fire that spread through the old Palace.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: Understand matching split tally receipts and the documented disposal decision that led to catastrophic fire.

segments.text: In 1834, Britain’s Parliament caught fire because workers were destroying old receipts.
For centuries, the government recorded payments with notches, then split the wood so both sides kept a matching record.
When that system became obsolete, two cartloads of sticks were left to dispose of.
Workers fed them into heating furnaces beneath the House of Lords.
A chimney fire smouldered under the chamber floor. Heat and smoke were noticed, but the burning continued.
Both parliamentary chambers were destroyed. Westminster Hall survived.
The dangerous part wasn’t keeping records on wood. It was choosing where to burn them.
